This checklist is intended only for self-questioning and does not constitute hiring criteria, a competency score, or an evaluative conclusion about the effectiveness of fire prevention inspection and fireground work. This page is written according to the United States O*NET-SOC 33-2022.00 "Forest Fire Inspectors and Prevention
Specialists" (the fixed index gives this asset a Chinese label meaning "fire inspector specialist"; the main subjects are enforcing fire prevention regulations, inspecting forest fire hazards and recommending fire prevention or control measures, and possibly reporting fire and weather conditions).

Paper-based fictional material｜Site A is a work area and its record shows uncleared combustible waste; B is a camp, notice N says it is closed today, and visitors are asking to enter; C is a lookout point, and M1/M2 both record a suspected smoke column in the same direction at 10:00, both lacking coordinates, and the exercise specifies that they are the same clue pending verification. Equipment E totals 18 items: 13 tagged as inspected, 3 pending inspection, and 2 out of service, while the plan needs 14 issuable items. The weather record has only the 10:00 temperature, with humidity and wind
speed missing. Exercise rules: only inspected items count as issuable, and pending-inspection and out-of-service items are not issued; the closure notice is not lifted by visitors' requests; missing information must not be filled in and a suspected clue must not be written up as a confirmed fire. Task｜Within 90 minutes, produce the P/N exception list, the E inventory calculation, and the M deduplication record, and write a handover summary; list the missing weather data and coordinates, and do not calculate a fire danger rating from missing items. All of this is paper records; finding a real fire or operating equipment is not required.

Fit signals｜O*NET points of note: face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (89%), teamwork being extremely important (90%), continuous contact with others (79%), telephone communication every day (77%), using email every day (75%), being outdoors exposed to all weather every day (68%), working indoors in an uncontrolled environment every day (68%), very great decision-making freedom (61%), making decisions every day (59%), leading or coordinating others being extremely important (57%), and dealing with the external public being important (51%). If you are willing to patrol and inspect outdoors over the long term according to regulations and checklists, can lead crews in fire prevention and suppression preparation, and speak to the public, this occupation's daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals｜O*NET also shows: decisions having a very important impact on the results of coworkers and the unit (93%), very high responsibility for the health and safety of others (77%), being in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day (69%), exposure to very hot or very cold temperatures more than once a week (68%), exposure to hazardous conditions more than once a week (54%), exposure to minor burns or cuts or bites or stings more than once a week (53%), exposure to distracting noise every day (52%), consequences of error being extremely serious (55%), working more than 40
hours (58%), conflict situations more than once a week (40%), and extremely fierce job competition (50%). Fire prevention inspection and patrol carry fireground, smoke, weather, and terrain risks, and hazard judgment and record errors can affect control and suppression decisions. If you find long-term outdoor and high-risk environments hard to bear, or lack patience for regulation enforcement, public communication, and precise records, treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Validation suggestions｜First complete the P/N/E/M paper records and independently recompute the 18 items and the shortfall of 1, and distinguish a suspected clue from a confirmed fire; paper results do not validate physical fitness, on-site safety, or enforcement qualifications. For real experience, check training and authorization separately.

The weather record has only the 10:00 temperature, with humidity and wind
speed missing. Exercise rules: only inspected items count as issuable, and pending-inspection and out-of-service items are not issued; the closure notice is not lifted by visitors' requests; missing information must not be filled in and a suspected clue must not be written up as a confirmed fire. All of this is paper records; finding a real fire or operating equipment is not required.

Occupational scope｜O*NET33-2022: enforcing forest fire prevention regulations, inspecting hazards, recommending prevention and control measures, and reporting fires and weather, and it also lists fireline crew direction, small fire suppression, and drone monitoring. The fixed Chinese label is retained as "fire inspector specialist." The task list does not confer enforcement, flight, or on-site command qualifications; independent investigation conclusions, major cross-agency coordination, and permitting authority must be checked against real job authorization.

entries: Fire prevention inspection and hazard remediation｜Stand, work area, and camp inspection｜Check combustible materials and burning and equipment and facility hazards according to regulations and checklists and propose remediation and prevention suggestions.

Patrol and fire discovery and reporting｜Patrol, lookout, and positioning｜Patrol and keep watch over the assigned area, discover fires and hazardous weather and terrain conditions, and position and report them.

Burn control and entry management｜Restricting access and burning and informing｜During high fire danger periods, restrict public access and burning, and check whether camps and users comply with forest use and fire prevention and sanitation rules.

Fire prevention outreach and on-site crew leadership｜Public education and crew training｜Explain fire prevention safety to the public and train crews; O*NET also lists fireline crew direction and small fire suppression, which must be undertaken according to real training and authorization.

Equipment and record management｜Protective equipment and ledgers｜Inspect and inventory suppression equipment and specialized protective equipment, arrange maintenance or request replenishment, and log and maintain the record ledger.

Weather and information and coordination｜Weather data and liaison and coordination｜Compile and report weather data such as temperature, humidity, wind direction and speed, and cloud cover, and liaise with crew members and emergency and fire service forces for coordination.

paragraphs:
Work context｜O*NET 33-2022.00 work context shows: the work combines patrol and inspection and on-site direction and public outreach, with outdoor work, teamwork, and decision responsibility standing out.
Communication and collaboration｜Face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (89%), teamwork being extremely important (90%), continuous contact with others (79%), telephone communication every day (77%), using email every day (75%).

Outdoors and environment｜Being outdoors exposed to all weather every day (68%), working indoors in an uncontrolled environment every day (68%), exposure to very hot or very cold temperatures at least once a week but not every day (68%), exposure to very bright or poorly lit conditions at least once a week but not every day (40%).

Hazards and protection｜Exposure to distracting noise every day (52%), exposure to contaminants every day (42%), exposure to hazardous equipment at least once a week but not every day (43%), exposure to hazardous conditions at least once a week but not every day (54%), wearing common protective equipment every day (38%), wearing specialized protective equipment at least once a week but not every day (35%).
Vehicles and equipment｜Being in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day (69%).

Decisions and responsibility｜Making decisions every day (59%), very great decision-making freedom (61%), decisions having a very important impact on the results of coworkers and the unit (93%), some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (44%), consequences of error being extremely serious (55%).

Leadership and influence｜Leading or coordinating others being extremely important (57%), very high responsibility for the health and safety of others (77%), very high responsibility for the work results of others (40%), dealing with the external public being important (51%), extremely fierce job competition (50%).
Time and physical effort｜A typical work week of more than 40
hours (58%), standing more than half the time (53%), walking or running more than half the time (51%), doing repetitive motions more than half the time (52%), using hands to handle, control, or feel objects about half the time (41%), bending or twisting the body about half the time (45%).

Other conditions｜Public speaking at least once a week but not every day (43%), writing letters and memos every day (33%), conflict situations at least once a week but not every day (40%), dealing with unpleasant or angry or discourteous people at least once a month but not every week (37%), physical proximity being slightly close (34%), working outdoors in a sheltered area at least once a month but not every week (24%). Percentages are respondents' category answers, not personal work hours or accident rates.

Environment and pace｜O*NET respondent context: outdoors in all weather every day 68%, indoors in an uncontrolled environment 68%, enclosed vehicles 69%, noise 52%; extreme temperatures at least once a week but not every day 68%, hazardous conditions 54%, minor injuries 53%; a typical work week of more than 40 hours 58%, standing more than half the time 53%, walking more than half the time 51%, repetitive motions more than half the time 52%. These are answers in the specified categories, not the workload of everyone, a physical intensity grade, or a ranking of peak fire-season intensity. Percentages are respondents' category answers, not personal work hours or accident rates.

Equipment material｜O*NET tasks specify maps and azimuth positioning, portable extinguishers and shovels and axes, inventory of items such as hoses and pumps, drone monitoring, and weather and records. The NWCG patrol guide requires equipment and communication conditions to be listed by task; this article does not treat an inferred list as the equipment every employer commonly uses or must carry, and provides no burn operations.
Patrol and lookout → Check hazards and burning → Propose remediation and prevention → Enforce control and inform → Inspect equipment and protective gear → Compile weather and report records

Quality suggestions｜Check hazard locations, equipment status, and weather and record sources according to the real institution's inspection, reporting, and authorization rules; keep the original records, leave a trail for corrections, do not treat after-the-fact fabrication as a supplementary entry, and do not categorically prohibit genuine error correction. Fireline crew leadership is an official task, and independent authority is checked separately.

Adjacent responsibility boundaries｜This page covers O*NET-SOC 33-2022.00; adjacent but different occupations include: Firefighters (on-site suppression and rescue work), Fire Inspectors and Investigators (building and facility fire inspection and fire-cause investigation), First-Line
Supervisors of Firefighting and Prevention Workers (shift and crew management), Emergency Management Directors (cross-departmental emergency coordination and plans), Fish and Game
Wardens (enforcement and patrol), Forest and Conservation Technicians (stand survey and tending and operational supervision), Forest and Conservation Workers (supervised physical work), and First-Line
Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers. These occupations differ from this one in authorization and outputs; matters involving command, investigation, and enforcement discretion are borne by the corresponding roles.

Boundary review points｜The following situations should be reported and escalated immediately: an incipient fire or spreading fire requiring reinforcements; personnel injured or trapped or missing; smoke and wind shifts threatening people and residential areas; unlawful burning or refusal to cooperate with access or conflict and threats; cross-region reinforcement and dispatch and unified command; and disputes over fire cause and penalties. The above are handled by the fire prevention and emergency lead, the fire command, and the competent authority according to regulations and plans.
Patrol → Inspect hazards → Propose remediation → Control and inform → Equipment and records → Report and coordinate

Difference from firefighters: firefighters produce on-site suppression and rescue work; this occupation's main outputs are enforcement of fire prevention regulations, inspection of fire hazards and remediation recommendations, patrol and fire reporting, burn control, and public outreach, and it takes part in suppression preparation and equipment and weather and record work.

Difference from fire-inspectors-and-investigators: the latter focus on fire code inspection of buildings and facilities and fire-cause investigation; this occupation focuses on fire hazard inspection of forests, woodlands, work areas, and camps, and on fire control, patrol, and outreach, while fire-cause investigation conclusions and penalty rulings are made by investigation and enforcement roles.

Adjacent comparison｜Firefighters focus on suppression and rescue, inspectors and investigators on building codes and fire-cause investigation, first-line supervisors on organizing people, and emergency management on cross-departmental coordination; this occupation focuses on forest fire prevention inspection and patrol and also lists fireline crew direction. The difference lies in the subject and the main outputs, and the tasks are not claimed to never overlap.

Difference from emergency-management-directors and first-line-supervisors-of-firefighting-and-prevention-
workers: the former are responsible for cross-departmental emergency coordination and plans and resource coordination; the latter are responsible for crews and shifts and safety and task assignment; this occupation centers on frontline inspection and patrol and control and outreach and records and executes tasks under plans and shift arrangements.

Comparison suggestions｜Check the actual proportions of inspection, patrol, outreach, and crew leadership, and check the high school/related experience/training conditions, outdoor costs, and authority; an official task list provides no local employer composition, task share, or uniform promotion guarantee.

Responsibility boundaries｜This occupation's list includes fireline crew direction, so not all crew leadership can be excluded; major fireground cross-agency coordination, investigation conclusions, and penalty authority are checked against the real position, jurisdiction, and institutional authorization, and a similar name does not confer the same authority.

AI task exposure｜Digital tools may assist with drone patrol and initial fire detection screening, fire danger rating and weather models and forecasts, GIS
and map positioning and route planning, imagery and patrol record organizing, drafting training and outreach materials, and automatic consolidation of ledgers and reports. But on-site patrol and hazard judgment, burn and access control and notification, incipient fire handling and personnel safety, inspection and maintenance of equipment and specialized protective gear, and violation correction and conflict handling remain the responsibility of inspectors and frontline personnel; task exposure does not equal job replacement, and tool output cannot replace field verification and on-site judgment.

Occupational definition｜According to the United States O*NET33-2022, this occupation enforces forest fire prevention regulations, inspects forest fire hazards and recommends fire prevention or control measures, and may report fires and weather; tasks also include crew training, fireline direction, small fire suppression, equipment inventory, and drone monitoring. The task description does not confer enforcement, flight, or command qualifications, and actual authority is checked against the real position.

Data and system thresholds｜Before adoption, verify: whether patrol and inspection and weather records can be traced back to person, time, place, and equipment; whether coordinates, maps, fire positioning, and ledger definitions are consistent; the permissions and retention periods for drone imagery and location and control data; data consistency and audit trails with dispatch, plan, and enforcement systems; and whether offline work can continue and original records be retained during network outages or equipment failures.

Human control points and manual review｜On-site patrol and hazard judgment, burn control and access restriction and notification, incipient fire handling and on-site safety, inspection and maintenance of equipment and specialized protective gear, violation correction and conflict handling, and weather and fire reporting must be completed by inspectors and frontline and crew-lead personnel; any tool-generated imagery screening, fire danger models, statistics, and report drafts must be checked by a human and leave a trail before use.

Residual responsibility｜Matters that must not be released automatically: the real judgment of fire danger and hazards, decisions and notification on control and access restriction, on-site handling of an incipient fire and personnel evacuation, requests for suppression and reinforcements and dispatch, and reporting and referral involving violations and fire cause. No tool output equals an inspection conclusion or a dispatch or enforcement decision.

Failure risk｜If tool output is not reviewed, it may lead to missed or misjudged hazards, inaccurate control scope, drone imagery misjudgments treated as reality, and distorted fire positioning and weather reporting, causing loss of fire control and personnel safety and compliance risks. Before rollout, clarify who reviews and against what original records and field verification.

Employment evidence boundary｜Employment and wage data for this occupation must be distinguished by definition: the United States figures from O*NET and BLS are estimates under a specific statistical definition and cannot be directly extrapolated to mainland China or other regions; China uses the industry-category average wage as a background proxy, which does not constitute an occupational wage conclusion. Everything generated should be traceable to original inputs and sources, and fluent wording must not be treated as correct evidence.

Tool exploration suggestions｜First check errors using fictional imagery indexes, weather records, map ledgers, and outreach drafts; real fire danger models, drone flight, and position deployment information are not automatically low risk. Adoption, flight, control, and dispatch are checked against real institutional systems and jurisdiction, and reversibility does not imply safety or permission.

Cross-market definition boundary｜Mainland China and the United States use different industry and occupational classification systems: mainland China publishes average wages of urban unit employees by national economic industry category and does not list this occupation separately; the United States gives estimates by SOC occupation and industry. The two cannot be spliced or converted, and an industry average cannot be used in place of an occupational wage.

Insufficient evidence: this page's check of the National Bureau of Statistics 2025 wage release obtained no mainland China occupational wage or employment value precisely corresponding to 33-2022; the industry proxy is not used as a fill-in.

Mainland China wage evidence review points｜This page provides only statistical definitions, industry background proxies, and a register of visible gaps; it does not provide an estimated salary for this occupation. Before using any value, first confirm whether its statistical definition (industry category / occupation), statistical period, unit of measurement, and covered population are comparable to this occupation.

United States check｜May2025 wages use the 33-2022 national row, and 2025—2035 employment uses the dedicated BLS projection; normal-hours wages and employment projections cover different populations, and the broad 33-2020 group or 33-2021 is not used as a fill-in.

China industry wages｜The National Bureau of Statistics publishes by urban unit industry category, and public administration, social security, and social organizations 119,465 yuan/year is only a non-private industry background and cannot be used to infer this occupation's employer composition or pay in China.

Insufficient evidence: no verifiable-by-occupation median wage for forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists was obtained for mainland China; the industry-category average is not used as a fill-in.

Mainland China wage evidence — statistical period｜The industry average wage is an annual figure (the values below are for 2025, released in 2026) and differs from the May 2025 point-in-time wage for the United States on this page; the two periods cannot be mixed.

Cross-market definition boundary｜Mainland China's industry average wage and the United States' occupational wage differ in statistical object, period, and definition; this page lists them separately with limitations noted, makes no currency conversion, and does not treat the industry average as an occupational wage.

China wage measurement｜The National Bureau of Statistics pre-tax annual total wage includes stipulated items such as wages, bonuses, and allowances; these differ from the OEWS normal-hours wage items, so the two are not directly comparable.

Insufficient evidence: no wage data for forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists verifiable by region or employment form was obtained for mainland China; individual quotes or secondhand accounts are not used as a fill-in.

China wage coverage｜In 2025, urban legal entities with 5 or more persons, excluding self-employed individuals and freelancers; employees must not be categorically excluded based on seasonal or scattered status.

OEWS covers the normal-hours pre-tax wages of full-time and part-time wage and salary employees and excludes the self-employed, overtime premium, non-production bonuses, and employer benefit costs; seasonal employees or on-call allowances must not be categorically excluded.
Statistical period｜Wages are May2025, the BLS employment base period is 2025 with projections for 2025—2035; O*NET still displays 2024—2034 and the two must not be mixed as the same period.

United States wage measurement｜OEWS annual wages are usually converted as hourly wage ×2,080 hours; the published hourly and annual wages are rounded, and seasonal employees' annual income must be checked against actual paid hours.

OEWS covers the normal-hours pre-tax wages of full-time and part-time wage and salary employees and excludes the self-employed, overtime premium, non-production bonuses, and employer benefit costs; seasonal employees or on-call allowances must not be categorically excluded.

United States wage evidence — occupational scope｜The values on this page correspond to SOC 33-2022 (Forest Fire Inspectors and Prevention Specialists); they exclude firefighters (33-2011), fire inspectors and investigators (33-2021), first-line supervisors of firefighting and prevention workers (33-1021), emergency management directors (11-9161), fish and game wardens (33-3031), forest and conservation technicians (19-4071), forest and conservation workers (45-4011), and first-line supervisors of farming, fishing, and forestry workers (45-1011). Wages cannot be mixed across occupations.

Statistical limitations｜OEWS sampling error and missing sub-categories must be checked in the specific tables; the OOH has verified local government and state government industry median wages, and other unverified directions retain their specific gaps. The EP figure of about 3,000 positions does not equal the OEWS employee count.

Conclusion｜The core difference between this occupation and adjacent occupations lies in authorization and outputs: this occupation handles fire prevention regulation enforcement and fire hazard inspection and remediation recommendations and patrol and fire reporting and burn control and public outreach and record reporting; firefighters produce on-site suppression and rescue work; fire inspectors and investigators produce building and facility fire inspection and fire-cause investigation; first-line supervisors of firefighting and prevention workers are responsible for shift and crew management; emergency management directors are responsible for cross-departmental emergency coordination and plans; fish and game wardens
are responsible for enforcement and patrol. Authorization and outputs differ in each case, so judgment and sign-off authority cannot be carried across roles.

Evidence note｜The comparison subjects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and official public materials and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent occupations and to support fit choices; they do not constitute qualification, hiring, or pay conclusions. The wages and employment of each occupation must be checked separately under their own SOC definition; this table makes no numerical comparison and does not treat one occupation's wage as a proxy for another.

Preface｜The following comparison is laid out in four columns: occupational direction — core work and outputs — key differences — who it suits better. These fire prevention and public safety positions often work together during emergencies and fire danger periods, but coordination does not mean they are interchangeable; when moving across directions, procedures, regulations, and qualification requirements must be relearned.

Centers on fire prevention regulation enforcement and fire hazard inspection and patrol and fire reporting and burn control and public outreach: hazard inspection and remediation recommendations, patrol and lookout and positioning and reporting, high-fire-danger-period access and burn control and notification, fire prevention education and training drills, inspection and recording of equipment and specialized protective gear, and weather and fire information reporting and coordination.

Better suited to people who are willing to patrol and inspect outdoors over the long term according to regulations and checklists, can face the public to enforce control and persuade, and bear public safety responsibility.

Outputs are inspection and control and patrol results: hazard ledgers and remediation recommendations, patrol and fire reports, control and notification records, equipment and gear inspection and ledgers, and weather and fire danger information reporting records.
This occupation: Forest Fire Inspectors and Prevention Specialists
Centers on on-site suppression and rescue work for fires and accidents: extinguishing, forcible entry, search and rescue, hazardous materials handling, and medical first aid assistance.

Better suited to people who focus on on-site suppression and rescue work and take orders; this occupation focuses on inspection and patrol and control and outreach and takes part in suppression preparation.
Outputs are suppression and rescue results: extinguishing, search and rescue, and hazardous materials handling records, rescuing trapped people, and on-site safety and equipment use records.
Firefighters

Centers on fire code inspection of buildings and facilities and fire-cause investigation: code compliance inspection and remediation requirements, and fire-cause examination and evidence collection and investigation reports.

Better suited to people who take responsibility for code inspection and fire-cause investigation and conclusions; this occupation focuses on fire hazard inspection and fire control in forests and woodlands.

Outputs are inspection and investigation conclusions: building and facility inspection reports and remediation requirements, fire-cause investigation conclusions and reports, and penalty and enforcement recommendations.
Fire Inspectors and Investigators
Centers on cross-departmental emergency coordination and plans and resource coordination: emergency plans and drills, resource and information coordination, and cross-agency command and liaison.

Better suited to people who take responsibility for emergency coordination and plans and resource coordination; this occupation executes frontline inspection and patrol and control under plans and dispatch.
Outputs are emergency coordination results: emergency plans and drill records, resource and information coordination and decisions, and cross-agency liaison and response reports.
Emergency Management Directors
Centers on shifts and crews and safety and task assignment: shift and task assignment, on-site safety and quality supervision, and personnel training and assessment.
Better suited to people who take responsibility for crew and shift management and on-site supervision; this occupation focuses on frontline inspection and patrol and control and outreach.
Outputs are frontline management results: shift and task and safety and quality records, training and assessment records, and incident handling and review records.
First-Line Supervisors of Firefighting and Prevention Workers
Centers on enforcement and patrol and case handling: patrol and enforcement procedures and evidence and discretion, and regulation outreach and case handling.

Better suited to people who take responsibility for enforcement and case discretion; this occupation focuses on fire prevention inspection and control and outreach, and violation correction is mainly persuasion and reporting.
Outputs are enforcement results: patrol and enforcement records, case and penalty documents, and regulation outreach and public notification records.
Fish and Game Wardens

Transition｜This page places adjacent positions side by side by authorization and outputs in order to help you judge which kind of fire prevention and public safety field work you want to invest in long term. Whichever direction you choose, what truly determines whether you can take the job is your understanding of regulations and plans and safety requirements, your ability to stay accurate and reviewable in outdoor and fireground and equipment environments, and passing institutional and employer training and assessment; interest questionnaires are only for raising questions.

Use tools in reversible assistance steps: imagery and record organizing, weather data entry, and map and ledger retrieval; hazard judgment and control and reporting are subject to verification by the crew lead.
Frontline inspection and patrol personnel

paragraphs: Boundary｜What this page lists are the more common failure types and control points for this occupation in fire prevention inspection, patrol, and suppression preparation, intended to help identify and manage risk; it does not constitute legal, operational safety, fire prevention, suppression, occupational health, or emergency management advice. Anything involving fires and casualties, equipment and specialized protective gear incidents, and cross-region dispatch and fire cause and penalty disputes should be handled by the person in charge, the fire prevention and emergency lead, and the competent authority according to regulations and plans.

Direct answer｜The core risk of this occupation is not "can you patrol" but four types of failure with heavier consequences: field and fireground safety failure (terrain and weather and smoke and equipment and vehicle accidents), fire and burning failure (hazards not found and burn control failure and reignition of embers and unlawful burning), inspection and record failure (hazard judgment and remediation recommendations and record ledgers and weather reporting errors), and control and conflict failure (restricting access and burning and weak enforcement and persuasion and conflicts with the public or contractors
).

Evidence scope｜Actual tasks and work context are taken from O*NET33-2022; patrol planning, communication, and the enforcement qualification boundary are taken from NWCG PMS456 March2018. The scenarios below are editorial designs, not accident case statistics, and no probabilities or health conclusions are derived.
Inspectors and frontline and crew-lead personnel; crew members and oneself

Working on steep slopes or slippery terrain or in severe weather or smoke or oxygen-deficient conditions, or improper use of equipment and vehicles; personal injury such as falls and falls from height and vehicle and equipment injuries and heatstroke and hypothermia and smoke inhalation

Editorial risk note｜The NWCG2018 patrol plan checks terrain and weather, communications, roads, and equipment, and adoption is decided by the responsible institution. For a direct threat, secure safety, call, and report first without waiting for the person in charge to confirm; this page provides no route or protection operating parameters.
Scenario｜Patrol continued along the original route under strong wind and smoke conditions, and one crew member developed breathing discomfort from smoke inhalation.
Inspectors and frontline personnel; crew members and the public and forest resources

Hazards not found or remediation recommendations inadequate, or fire-season burning and access control poorly enforced, or embers and cigarettes and equipment igniting; fire occurrence and spread, endangering people and resources and residential areas

China 2026 regulations｜Report a fire immediately and secure personnel refuge first; anyone without professional training must not be assigned to fight it directly, and participation follows unified command. Reading the material does not confer suppression qualifications; this page provides no suppression parameters, and actual emergency response is checked against the system.
Scenario｜A burning complaint was received during the fire danger period but no timely on-site check was made, and a fire broke out hours later and spread to the work area.
Inspectors and the person in charge and the operator; control and suppression decisions and the definition of responsibility

Hazard judgment and remediation recommendations and record ledgers and weather reporting incomplete or untrue, or position and fire reports inaccurate; the basis for control and dispatch and reviews is distorted, affecting the suppression window and the definition of responsibility

Record according to checklists and standards and review, report weather and fire information truthfully and promptly, and keep the original records; when major record or reporting problems are found, review, correct, and report immediately according to procedures
Scenario｜The inspection record did not state the hazard location and remediation deadline, so the responsible party and remediation requirements could not be defined during the review.
Inspectors and the public and contractors; public safety and institutions and individuals

Access and burning restrictions and remediation requirements poorly enforced through persuasion, or conflict and threats with the public or contractors; unlawful burning and entry causing fires and compliance and legal disputes and personal safety risk

Editorial risk note｜NWCG points out that enforcement tasks require the corresponding qualification from the responsible institution; record the restriction and the visitor's request, refer conflicts to the institution's responsible or enforcement personnel, and do not expand authority on one's own.
Scenario｜A tourist asked to stop burning in a no-burn zone refused and insulted the inspector, and the inspector handled it alone, escalating the conflict.
Inspectors and crew members; oneself and others

Equipment and specialized protective gear inspection or maintenance inadequate, or damaged and failed equipment still in use; equipment failure affects suppression and patrol effectiveness and causes personal injury

Inspect, inventory, and record equipment status according to procedures, and take damaged equipment out of service and report or replace it according to procedures; take defective equipment out of service, report it, and record it immediately
Scenario｜Hose and extinguisher pressure were not checked before patrol, and equipment failure during handling of an incipient fire delayed the response.
Inspectors and crew members and facilities; oneself and the public

Long hours in the field and stationing and duty and repetitive motions and prolonged standing, or risks in lookout tower and facility and fence maintenance; musculoskeletal strain and fatigue-related errors and work injuries and facility hazards

Editorial risk note｜O*NET reports 58% for a typical work week of more than 40 hours and requirements for prolonged standing and walking; specific rotation, health, and facility arrangements are checked with the real employer, and this page makes no medical judgment.
Scenario｜After several consecutive days of stationing and night duty, a long-distance hiking patrol was still assigned, and one crew member sprained an ankle on the way back due to fatigue.

values: Fictional patrol material

Paper-based fictional material｜Site A is a work area and its record shows uncleared combustible waste; B is a camp, notice N says it is closed today, and visitors are asking to enter; C is a lookout point, and M1/M2 both record a suspected smoke column in the same direction at 10:00, both lacking coordinates, and the exercise specifies that they are the same clue pending verification. Equipment E totals 18 items: 13 tagged as inspected, 3 pending inspection, and 2 out of service, while the plan needs 14 issuable items. The weather record has only the 10:00 temperature, with humidity and wind
speed missing. Exercise rules: only inspected items count as issuable, and pending-inspection and out-of-service items are not issued; the closure notice is not lifted by visitors' requests; missing information must not be filled in and a suspected clue must not be written up as a confirmed fire.
All statuses and deduplication relationships are governed by the exercise.
Calculation and recording task

Task｜Within 90 minutes, produce the P/N exception list, the E inventory calculation, and the M deduplication record, and write a handover summary; list the missing weather data and coordinates, and do not calculate a fire danger rating from missing items. All of this is paper records; finding a real fire or operating equipment is not required.
Keep the sources, the original records, and the to-be-confirmed items.
Reviewable reference deliverable

Reference deliverable｜E has 13 issuable, the plan needs 14, and the shortfall is 14−13=1; pending inspection 3 and out of service 2 are listed separately, and 13+3+2=18. The A waste is registered as a hazard pending review as the exercise specifies, B stays closed and the visitor request is recorded and handed to the person in charge; M1/M2 keeps the original records and are linked as the same clue pending verification, and must not be recorded as two fires or one confirmed fire. Coordinates, humidity, and wind speed are to be supplemented, and the current material cannot be used to calculate a fire danger rating. The shortfall, pending-inspection, and out-of-service items
are handed to the person in charge, and statuses are not changed on one's own.
Check against 13+3+2=18 and 14−13=1, and state clearly that the fire danger rating cannot be calculated.
Paper boundaries

Paper boundaries｜The exercise statuses are only for practice and are not statutory standards, a fire danger algorithm, or work authorization. The exercise does not carry out suppression, access-restriction enforcement, drone flight, equipment operation, or on-site investigation, and does not confer judgment or sign-off authority; the actual position follows employer training, effective procedures, and authorization.

entries.answer:
According to O*NET-SOC 33-2022.00, this occupation enforces fire prevention regulations, inspects forest fire hazards, and recommends fire prevention or control measures, and may report fire and weather conditions; common job titles include fire prevention management officer, fire prevention officer, fire prevention technician, forest officer, and forest district ranger. The work includes hazard inspection and remediation recommendations, patrol and lookout and fire positioning and reporting, high-fire-danger-period access and burn control and notification, fire prevention outreach and training drills, inspection and recording and maintenance of equipment and specialized protective gear, and weather data and fire danger
information consolidation and coordinated reporting. It excludes unified command of major cross-region firegrounds and national-level dispatch, fire-cause investigation conclusions and administrative penalties and final determination of legal application, stand management and harvest and long-term planning decisions, scientific research and plan formulation, environmental media sampling and monitoring, and the final decision on permit approval.
entries.question: What does this occupation actually do?

entries.answer: Firefighters produce on-site suppression and rescue work; fire inspectors and investigators produce building and facility fire code inspection and fire-cause investigation; first-line supervisors of firefighting and prevention workers are responsible for shifts and crews and safety and task assignment; emergency management directors are responsible for cross-departmental emergency coordination and plans and resource coordination; fish and game wardens are responsible for enforcement and patrol. This occupation handles fire prevention regulation enforcement and fire hazard inspection and remediation recommendations and patrol and fire reporting and burn control and public outreach and record reporting.

subject.summary: According to the United States O*NET-SOC33-2022, this occupation enforces forest fire prevention regulations, inspects hazards, recommends prevention and control measures, and reports fires and weather; it also lists crew training, fireline direction, equipment inventory, and drone monitoring. The fixed Chinese label means "fire inspector specialist," and the main subject is forest fire prevention. The task list does not confer enforcement, flight, or command qualifications, and real employer training and authorization must be checked.
